title: Extraction and uses of metals
learningObjective: Know that most metals are extracted from ores found in the Earth’s crust and that unreactive metals are often found as the uncombined element; Explain how the method of extraction of a metal is related to its position in the reactivity series, illustrated by carbon extraction for iron and electrolysis for aluminium; Be able to comment on a metal extraction process, given appropriate information (detailed knowledge of the processes used in the extraction of a specific metal is not required); Explain the uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel in terms of their properties (the types of steel will be limited to low-carbon (mild), high-carbon and stainless); Know that an alloy is a mixture of a metal and one or more elements, usually other metals or carbon; Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals

sections.title: Extraction and Uses of Metals
sections.markdown:
Look around: aircraft overhead, cables strung between pylons, rails,
reinforcing bars, coins in your pocket. Metals carry modern life — and
almost every one of them began as rock dug out of the ground. Very few
occur as the pure element ready to use. The rest are locked into
compounds in the Earth's crust, and the branch of chemistry that wins
them back is **extraction**: redox reactions run on an industrial
scale, using exactly the [[reactivity-series]] logic you built in
Chapter 14 (u2:c14).

One idea organises the whole chapter. A metal's position in the
reactivity series decides how hard it is to extract — and therefore
how it is extracted, and roughly what it costs. Gold sits so low that
it can be found [[native]], as the uncombined element, glinting in a
pan; iron needs a furnace fed by carbon; aluminium demands huge
quantities of electricity. Extraction method, price and even the
metal's everyday job all trace back to that one ranking.

The chapter runs in two halves. First, extraction: what an [[ore]] is,
why carbon can strip oxygen from some metal oxides but not others, why
electrolysis takes over above zinc, and how to reason your way through
an extraction process you have never seen. Then the payoff: what the
extracted metals are actually *for* — the uses of aluminium, copper,
iron and steel, the alloy families (brass, bronze, the steels), and
why hammering other elements into a metal makes it harder. Each half
is examined every year in Paper 2C, and the command word is usually
"explain": explain the method from the position, explain the use from
the property, explain the hardness from the structure.

:::prior-knowledge
Four earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 14 (u2:c14) you need
the reactivity series itself — especially carbon's reference position
— and the redox vocabulary: oxidation as gain of oxygen or loss of
electrons, reduction as the reverse, and the agent terms. From
Chapter 9 (u1:c09) you need metallic structure: a regular lattice of
positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons, because the
explanation of alloy hardness is pure lattice reasoning. From
Chapter 10 (u1:c10) you need electrolysis of molten ionic compounds —
electrodes, half-equations and which electrode attracts which ion —
because that is literally how aluminium is won. Equations throughout
assume the balancing and state-symbol skills of Chapter 5 (u1:c05).
:::

:::exam-hint
Every objective in this chapter is chemistry-only: all six are
assessed in Paper 2C and none in Paper 1C or the double award. The
recurring question shapes are: explain why a metal is extracted by
carbon or by electrolysis from its position in the series; comment on
an unfamiliar extraction process using information printed in the
question; explain a use of aluminium, copper, iron or a steel from its
properties; and explain why an alloy is harder than the pure metal in
terms of the lattice. Each shape gets its own coaching as the chapter
goes.
:::

:::misconception
"Extracting a metal means separating it from the rock physically —
like sieving sand from gravel." For most metals that is impossible,
because the metal is not sitting in the rock as metal: it is chemically
combined inside mineral compounds such as oxides or sulfides. Winning
the metal is a *chemical* reduction — removing oxygen or adding
electrons — not a physical separation. Physical methods alone only
ever work for the unreactive metals that occur native, such as gold.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.22C orientation items. Before moving on,
say in one sentence what an ore is, and in one more why gold can be
found as the uncombined element while iron cannot. If both sentences
come out cleanly, the chapter's foundation is laid.
:::

sections.title: Extracting Metals from Their Ores
sections.markdown:
The Earth's crust holds most metals in combination with other
elements — as oxides, sulfides, carbonates and more. An individual
metal compound found in rock is a **[[mineral]]**. Two
iron-containing minerals make the idea concrete: one is iron sulfide,
FeS₂, and another is an iron oxide with formula Fe₃O₄. In real rock
these minerals are never neat and pure; they are scattered through
unwanted material.

An **[[ore]]** is a rock that contains enough of a metal-containing
mineral to make extracting the metal worthwhile. That definition has
two halves and both matter: the metal must be *there*, and there must
be *enough of it* for the process to pay for itself. Most metals are
extracted from ores found in the Earth's crust — but not all. A few
very unreactive metals, gold most famously, are found **[[native]]**:
existing naturally as the uncombined element, no chemistry required to
free them. Silver and copper are sometimes found native too, though
much more rarely — their slight reactivity means nearly all of their
atoms have combined with something over geological time.

Many ores contain the metal as an oxide already, or as a compound that
converts easily to one. Metal sulfides are the easy case: heating the
sulfide in air — a process known as **[[roasting]]** — converts it to
the oxide. The conversion for the zinc
sulfide ore shows the pattern:

2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g)

Zinc sulfide gains oxygen; the sulfur leaves as sulfur dioxide gas.
Roasting is the standard bridge from sulfide ore
to oxide, because the oxide is the starting point for the extraction
methods of the next sections.

:::did-you-know
The price of a metal reflects its ore: how common the ore is, and how
hard the metal is to extract from it. A common ore plus an easy
carbon-reduction drives the price down; a rare ore plus an
electricity-hungry extraction drives it up. That is why the extraction
method and the market price tell the same story from two directions.
:::

:::exam-hint
You are not required to remember the names of the ores or minerals —
examiners supply any mineral formulae you need. What you *are*
expected to know is the vocabulary and the logic: ore as
worthwhile-enough rock, native as uncombined element, and the fact
that most metals must be extracted from ores in the crust while
unreactive metals may occur uncombined. A two-mark "what is an ore"
question wants both halves of the definition — enough mineral, worth
extracting.
:::

:::misconception
"Gold is found native because it is dense and heavy, so it settles out
of rock." Density has nothing to do with it — panning gold works only
*because* it is already uncombined metal. Gold occurs native because
it is so unreactive: it has never combined with oxygen or sulfur in
the crust. A reactive metal such as sodium cannot be found native at
any density, because it has all reacted long ago.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.22C items. Try these cold: define an ore in
one sentence including both halves of the definition; name two metals
often found native and the property that explains it; write the
equation for roasting zinc sulfide in air. If the equation balances
with the right state symbols, this section is secure.
:::

sections.title: Extracting the Metal
sections.markdown:
Extraction always ends the same way: the metal's compound is turned
into the metal itself. In the oxide ores that dominate this chapter,
that means removing oxygen — and removing oxygen is
**[[reduction]]**. In the electron picture it means the same thing
from the other side: the metal in an ore exists as positive ions, and
to produce the neutral metal those ions must gain electrons. Reduction,
twice over, in both vocabularies of Chapter 14 (u2:c14).

That single sentence is the hinge of the whole topic, so it is worth
restating slowly. Iron(III) oxide contains Fe³⁺ ions; aluminium oxide
contains Al³⁺ ions. Extraction supplies electrons to those ions —
with carbon as the electron donor where possible, or with electricity
where not — and the neutral metal comes out. Every method you meet in
this chapter is just a different answer to one question: *what will
force electrons onto this metal ion?* How expensive that answer is
depends on how reactive the metal is, which is the next section's
subject.

The second half of the chapter turns from *getting* metals to *using*
them, and its objectives are worth stating in full now. You must be
able to explain the uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel in terms
of their properties, where the steel types are limited to three:
low-carbon (mild) steel, high-carbon steel and stainless steel. You
must know that an alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other
elements, usually other metals or carbon. And you must be able to
explain why alloys are harder than the pure metals they are made from
— an argument conducted entirely in the lattice language of
Chapter 9 (u1:c09).

If the oxidation/reduction vocabulary feels shaky, go back and re-read
Chapter 14 (u2:c14) before continuing: extraction questions are redox
questions, and the examiner's mark scheme uses those exact words.

:::exam-hint
The three objectives carried here are the "comment on" and "explain
the uses" family — the part of the chapter where examiners give you a
process or a metal you may never have met and expect you to reason
from principles. Detailed knowledge of any specific extraction plant
is *not* required. What earns the marks: spot the reduction, name the
reducing agent, link a property (density, conductivity, strength,
corrosion resistance) to a use, and describe the alloy lattice when
hardness is asked. Practise reading unfamiliar information calmly —
that skill *is* the objective.
:::

:::misconception
"Extracting copper from copper oxide is oxidation, because oxygen is
involved." The presence of oxygen in the *reactant* does not make the
process oxidation — watch what happens *to* the metal compound: it
*loses* oxygen, so the metal oxide is reduced. It is the reducing
agent (carbon, say) that is oxidised, by gaining the oxygen the metal
gave up. Direction of oxygen travel decides the labels, and the metal
always travels out of the ore by reduction.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.25C/2.26C/2.27C orientation items. In one
sentence each: what always happens chemically when a metal is
extracted from its oxide; what three types of steel the course limits
you to; what an alloy is. If the third sentence says "mixture of a
metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or
carbon", you are word-perfect for the mark scheme.
:::

sections.title: Metals Below Carbon in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
Take a metal oxide — iron(III) oxide, say — and ask what has to happen
to leave pure metal behind. The oxygen must go. **Reduction** is
the name for removal of oxygen, so obtaining a metal from its oxide is
always a reduction of the metal compound. That is the oxygen-language
statement; here is the same fact in electron language, and you need
both for the exam.

Metals exist as positive ions in their ionic compounds: iron(III)
oxide is Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ packed in a lattice, with no neutral iron atoms
anywhere. To produce the metal, each positive ion must be supplied
with enough electrons to balance its charge — Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe.
Addition of electrons is also called [[reduction]], so the two definitions
agree perfectly: removing oxygen from the oxide *is* giving electrons
back to the metal ion. The extracted metal is simply the ore's ions
re-clothed in their electrons.

This section covers the metals sitting *below* carbon in the
[[reactivity-series]] — zinc, iron, copper and the rest. The position
matters because carbon can only do the reducing job for metals it is
more reactive than: carbon takes oxygen from an oxide only if carbon
outranks the metal in the series. For everything below carbon, that
condition holds, and heating the oxide with carbon is the cheap route
to the metal. How that plays out for iron — and why aluminium needs
something far more aggressive — is the next section's economics.

:::exam-hint
Definition questions on reduction appear in extraction contexts every
year, and the mark scheme accepts either wording: "loss of oxygen" or
"gain of electrons". The safest answers give both, matched to the
reaction in front of you: the metal oxide is reduced because it loses
oxygen — and, in electron terms, because the metal ion gains
electrons. If asked about the metal ion specifically, the electron
version is the one that scores.
:::

:::misconception
"Reduction means the metal gets smaller or lighter." Reduction has
nothing to do with size — the word refers to the *oxide being reduced
back to the metal*, the ore's mass of oxygen leaving. Iron(III) oxide reduces to rather less iron, but the chemical meaning
is oxygen loss and electron gain, not shrinkage. Anchoring the word to
oxygen-and-electrons, rather than to everyday "reducing" imagery,
keeps every extraction answer on track.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.23C items. Complete these sentences aloud:
obtaining a metal from its oxide is called ______ because ______; in
electron terms the metal ion ______ electrons to become ______. Then
say why carbon can reduce the oxides of zinc and iron but not of
aluminium — if your answer uses the words "above" or "below" carbon in
the reactivity series, you have the organizing idea.
:::

sections.title: Methods of Extraction and the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
How a metal is extracted depends, to a large extent, on its position in
the [[reactivity-series]] — because the position decides which
chemical or electrical process can do the reduction, and every process
costs money. A manufacturer wants the cheapest method that works, and
two costs dominate: the cost of **energy** and the cost of the
**reducing agent**. Those two numbers, run against the reactivity
series, explain the entire map of extraction methods.

For a metal below carbon, heating the oxide with carbon wins on both
counts: coke is cheap, and a furnace is cheaper than an electrolysis
hall. The extraction of iron is the flagship example. A main ore of
iron contains a high percentage of iron(III) oxide, and carbon strips
the oxygen away when heated:

Fe₂O₃(s) + 3C(s) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO(g)

Read the equation as the redox story it is. Carbon is above iron in
the series, so it takes the oxygen for itself: the iron(III) oxide is
**reduced** to iron, the carbon is **oxidised** to carbon monoxide,
and the carbon is therefore the [[reducing-agent]] — the substance
that removes the oxygen (and, in electron terms, supplies the
electrons) while being oxidised itself.

The real industrial process runs in a [[blast-furnace]], and it is a
step more subtle than the simple equation above. Other reactions occur
inside the furnace, and the main reducing agent in practice is
actually carbon monoxide, formed from the coke, which then carries the
oxygen away from the iron oxide:

Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO₂(g)

Same redox bookkeeping, same product: the oxide loses oxygen, the
reducing agent gains it. That is as far as the course goes — the full
internal choreography of the furnace is not required.

:::exam-hint
In the exam you will never be asked to reproduce the blast furnace in
detail — the syllabus says detailed knowledge of specific extraction
processes is not required. What you must be able to do is *comment*
on a process you are handed: identify what is reduced, what is
oxidised, which substance is the reducing agent, and why the method
suits the metal's reactivity. Also expect the two-cost question:
extraction choices come down to the cost of energy and the cost of the
reducing agent — quoting either one alone loses the pairing mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Carbon reduces iron(III) oxide because carbon is hotter than the
furnace, or because carbon is heavier." The reduction happens because
carbon is *more reactive* than iron — higher in the reactivity series
— so carbon out-competes iron for the oxygen. Temperature is the
condition that lets the reaction proceed at a useful rate, not the
cause of the oxygen transfer. Reactivity ranking, not heat alone,
decides who takes the oxygen.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.23C/2.24C items. Write the equation for
heating iron(III) oxide with carbon, with state symbols, and label the
substance reduced, the substance oxidised and the reducing agent.
Then, in one sentence, name the two economic factors that decide the
cheapest extraction method. Finally: the main reducing agent inside an
operating blast furnace is not carbon itself — name it and write its
reduction equation.
:::

sections.title: Metals Above Carbon in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
Above zinc in the reactivity series, carbon's reducing power runs out.
Ores of metals higher than zinc cannot be reduced by carbon at
reasonable temperatures: those metals are more reactive than carbon,
so carbon simply cannot take their oxygen away. For potassium,
sodium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium, the winning method is
**electrolysis** — the method that never fails, because electrons are
supplied directly by the power supply rather than borrowed from a
reactive element. Iron and all other metals *could* also be extracted
by electrolysis, but the process is so expensive that it is used only
when it has to be.

Aluminium is the case to know. It is extracted by the electrolysis of
aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, dissolved in a molten salt called
**[[cryolite]]**. The dissolved oxide behaves exactly like the molten
electrolytes of Chapter 10 (u1:c10): aluminium ions migrate to the
cathode and are discharged as metal; oxide ions migrate to the anode
and are discharged as oxygen gas. The two half-equations carry the
whole story:

At the cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (**[[reduction]]**)

At the anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (**[[oxidation]]**)

Molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.

:::key-point
The cryolite is there to make the process economical. Aluminium oxide
melts at over 2000 °C — far too hot to run an electrolysis cell. Dissolved
in molten cryolite, the whole process runs at around 1000 °C instead.
That saves an enormous amount of energy, and energy is money: the
mixture, not the oxide alone, is what makes aluminium extraction
commercially possible at all.
:::

Even so, the process demands huge amounts of electricity, which makes
aluminium expensive. The price is a redox consequence: aluminium has
to be extracted by electrolysis, while iron is simply heated with
carbon — so aluminium costs much more than iron even though aluminium
is *more abundant* in the Earth's crust. Abundance never sets the
price; the reactivity series, through the extraction it forces, does.

A few awkward metals need a third route. Titanium, for example, is
extracted by heating its compound with a more reactive metal —
effectively buying the reduction from a metal that outranks titanium.
That is expensive too, and for a built-in reason: the more reactive
metal itself first had to be extracted by an expensive process, and
its cost is baked into the titanium's.

:::exam-hint
The aluminium question is a guaranteed Paper 2C shape. The full-mark
chain: name the electrolyte (aluminium oxide dissolved in molten
cryolite); state cryolite's job (lowers the operating temperature from
over 2000 °C to around 1000 °C, saving energy); give both
half-equations with the correct charges, electrons and gas; and label
cathode as reduction, anode as oxidation. For titanium-style
processes, the expected comment is the expense chain — a more reactive
metal does the reducing, and that metal had to be expensively
extracted itself.
:::

:::misconception
"Cryolite is a catalyst for the electrolysis." Cryolite changes no
reaction rate and is not consumed as a catalyst would be — it is a
solvent that dissolves the aluminium oxide so the ions can move at a
*lower temperature*. The saving is thermodynamic bookkeeping (a
1000 °C cell instead of a 2000 °C melt), not catalysis. Candidates who
write "catalyst" hand the examiner an easy mark to refuse.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.23C/2.24C items. Cover the page and
reproduce: the electrolyte composition, cryolite's purpose with both
temperatures, and both half-equations with electrode names. Then
answer in one sentence: why is aluminium more expensive than iron even
though the crust holds more of it? If your answer names electrolysis
versus carbon reduction, the economics have landed.
:::

sections.title: Alloys
sections.markdown:
Pure metals are rarely what products are made of — most metal objects
around you are mixtures, and the mixture is the point. An
**[[alloy]]** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements,
usually other metals or carbon. Two names carry the definition: **[[brass]]**
is a mixture of copper and zinc, and steel is an alloy of iron with
carbon. Both are made the same way — the elements are melted together
and mixed — and both behave differently from their pure parents.

The difference shows up as hardness, and the reason is pure lattice
geometry. Recall the metallic model from Chapter 9 (u1:c09): a pure
metal is a regular lattice of identical positive ions surrounded by
delocalised electrons, and that regularity is exactly what makes pure
metals soft. When a force is applied, whole planes of ions can slide
over one another and settle into new positions — the metal bends or
dents rather than shatters. Picture a neatly stacked rack of
identical balls: rows slide easily because every ball lines up with
the next.

Now stir differently sized atoms into the lattice, which is what
making an alloy does. In an alloy, the different metals or elements
have slightly differently sized atoms, so the regular arrangement
breaks up. The rows no longer line up; a sliding plane hits a
misfit atom almost immediately and jams. It becomes much more
difficult for the layers of ions to slide over each other — and that
is the whole answer to why alloys are harder than the pure metals
they are made from. The delocalised electrons are still there (the
alloy still conducts, still shines), but the slip-planes are wrecked.

Keep the definition tight as well as the explanation. "A mixture of a
metal and one or more elements, usually other metals or carbon" is
the exact wording the mark scheme wants: the base must be a *metal*,
the added elements are *usually* other metals or carbon — carbon in
the steels is the standard example of the exception — and "mixture"
matters because no chemical bonds rearrange; it is a blended
structure, not a compound.

:::exam-hint
The alloy-hardness question is marked in a fixed three-step chain:
(1) an alloy contains atoms of different sizes; (2) the regular
lattice arrangement is disrupted, so the layers cannot slide over
each other easily; (3) therefore the alloy is harder than the pure
metal. Write all three steps — answers that jump from "different
atoms" straight to "harder" drop the middle, mechanism mark every
time. And never explain hardness with the electrons: the sliding
layers of *ions* are the moving parts.
:::

:::misconception
"Alloys are compounds, because the elements are chemically bonded in a
fixed ratio." An alloy is a *mixture* — the added atoms sit in the
metal's lattice without forming new compounds, and their proportions
can be varied continuously (mild and high-carbon steels differ only in
carbon percentage, as the next sections show). Compounds have fixed
formulae and rearranged bonding; alloys have tunable recipes and an
unchanged metallic lattice with some atoms swapped in.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.26C/2.27C items. State the alloy definition
word-perfect, then give the two named examples with their
compositions (brass; steel). Finally, explain in three steps why an
alloy is harder than the pure metal — check your middle step mentions
layers of ions failing to slide. If any step says "because the atoms
are bigger", rebuild it: *differently sized*, not bigger.
:::

sections.title: Uses of Aluminium
sections.markdown:
Brass and steel opened the alloy story; three more named alloys
complete the catalogue the exam expects. **Bronze** is a mixture
of copper and tin — humanity's oldest engineered alloy, and still the
name given to that copper-tin family today. **Stainless steel**
is an alloy of iron with chromium and usually nickel: the chromium
contribution is what makes it "stainless", a story told properly in
the steel section. And **[[cupronickel]]** — the mixture of copper
and nickel — is usually used to make "silver" coins: the coinage in
your pocket that looks like silver contains no silver at all, just a
copper-nickel blend tuned to look and wear like it.

Each of these earns its place by combining its parents' virtues. The
copper in bronze and cupronickel contributes workability and
corrosion resistance; the tin hardens the **[[bronze]]**, the nickel toughens
and silvers the coinage. Stainless steel is the same design logic
applied to iron, whose rusting habit is exactly the weakness
**[[stainless-steel]]** patches. Notice the pattern across every alloy met
so far — brass, bronze, cupronickel, the steels: take a useful but
flawed pure metal, dissolve in a second element, and repair a specific
weakness. That design pattern is the "explain the use" objective in
miniature, and the steel kinds are where it is examined hardest.

:::exam-hint
Alloy-composition questions are recall-for-one-mark items: bronze is
copper *and tin*; stainless steel is iron *with chromium (and usually
nickel)*; cupronickel is copper *and nickel* and is the coinage
alloy; brass is copper *and zinc*. The commonest lost mark is writing
"bronze is a mixture of metals" — true but unscored. Name the
elements, and for stainless steel remember the chromium is the
anti-rust ingredient the examiner asks about next.
:::

:::misconception
"'Silver' coins contain silver, because that is what they are called."
The silvery colour comes from the cupronickel blend — copper and
nickel are both silvery-grey metals, and mixed they mimic silver
closely enough for everyday coinage. Coinage metals are chosen for
durability, wear resistance and modest cost, not for precious-metal
content. Treat the name as appearance, never as composition.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.25C/2.26C items. From memory, give the
composition of bronze, stainless steel and cupronickel, and say which
one lives in your pocket and why it is there. Then check the design
pattern: for each alloy, name the weakness of the base metal that the
added element repairs. If stainless steel's answer is "rusting", you
are ready for the steel section.
:::

sections.title: Properties and Uses of Some Metals
sections.markdown:
Aluminium's job list follows directly from four properties — and from
one honest weakness. Pure aluminium is not very strong, so
**aluminium alloys** are normally used instead: the metal can be
strengthened by adding other elements such as silicon, copper or
magnesium. This is the [[alloy]] logic of the last section doing
commercial work — keep aluminium's gifts, patch its softness.

The gifts: aluminium has a **low density** (about a third of steel's),
it is a **good conductor of electricity and of heat**, and it
**resists corrosion**. Each property buys a use. Planes are built
from aluminium alloys because low density is everything when something
must fly, and the alloys supply the strength pure aluminium lacks.
Overhead electricity cables carry aluminium — excellent conductivity
at low mass — and the cable design shows the alloy thinking again:
the aluminium is strengthened by a core of steel, marrying
conductivity to tensile strength in one cable. Pots and pans use the
other two gifts: heat conducted quickly to the food, and no corrosion
from anything cooked in the pan.

The corrosion resistance has a mechanism worth stating precisely,
because examiners ask for it. Aluminium reacts with oxygen in the air
instantly — but the product is a very thin, very strong layer of
aluminium oxide on the surface. The layer clings tight, is
impermeable, and prevents anything else reaching the metal underneath
and reacting with it. So the metal protects itself: the corrosion
product *is* the coating. Compare iron, whose rust flakes off and lets
attack continue — aluminium's oxide layer is the difference between
corrosion that stops and corrosion that spreads.

:::exam-hint
"Explain why aluminium is used for X" questions are marked
property-by-property: link *low density* to aircraft and cable
weight, *conducts electricity* to cables, *conducts heat* to
cookware, *resists corrosion* to outdoor and kitchen durability — and
where strength appears, credit the *alloying* (silicon, copper or
magnesium added; steel core in cables). The corrosion explanation
must mention the thin aluminium oxide layer and that it prevents
further reaction — "aluminium does not react" is the refused answer,
because it does, immediately and usefully.
:::

:::misconception
"Aluminium resists corrosion because it is unreactive." Aluminium is
actually near the *top* of the reactivity series — far more reactive
than iron. Its corrosion resistance comes from the behaviour of its
oxide product, not from any reluctance to react: it reacts so fast
with air that a protective oxide film seals the surface before
anything deeper is touched. Reactive metal, protective product — the
paradox resolves in the oxide layer, and stating both halves is the
full-mark answer.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.25C items. List aluminium's three selling
properties, then assign each to one use (planes, cables, pans). Now
the mechanism: explain corrosion resistance in two sentences — the
instant oxide formation and the barrier it creates. Finally, why is
pure aluminium rarely used structurally, and what is done about it?
If the second half of your answer names alloying additions, this
section is banked.
:::

sections.title: Properties and Uses of Different Kinds of Steel
sections.markdown:
Iron is the world's most important alloy base. There are many alloys
of iron containing various proportions of carbon and sometimes other
metals, and an alloy of iron with carbon is called **[[steel]]**. The
course needs three kinds, distinguished almost entirely by carbon
percentage — a perfect demonstration that alloy recipes are tunable,
not fixed.

**Mild steel** — low-carbon steel — contains up to about 0.25%
carbon. That small addition increases the hardness and strength of
the iron usefully while leaving the metal workable: **[[mild-steel]]**
is strong, and can be easily hammered into various shapes (**[[malleable]]**)
and drawn into wires (**[[ductile]]**). Those properties buy it a
huge workload — nails, car bodies, ship building, girders and bridges
among many others. Its weaknesses are equally specific: it rusts when
exposed to oxygen and water (the enemy from Chapter 14, u2:c14), and
it is about three times denser than aluminium. That density figure is
why some car bodies are made from aluminium instead: the body will
not rust, and because the car is lighter, less fuel has to be used —
two advantages against a cost, which is exactly how materials
engineers argue.

**High-carbon steel** contains about 0.6–1.2% carbon (the amounts
are variable), and usually small amounts of manganese as well. More
carbon makes the steel harder and more resistant to wear than mild
steel — but also more **brittle**: not as malleable and ductile. Hard
and wear-resistant is the spec sheet of a cutting tool, and that is
its home: **[[high-carbon-steel]]** is used for cutting tools. The
malleability that mild steel spends on girders is traded away for an
edge that stays sharp.

**Stainless steel** is iron alloyed with chromium and often
nickel, and its magic is borrowed chemistry: chromium forms a strong
oxide layer in the same way aluminium does, and that oxide layer
protects the iron underneath too, so **[[stainless-steel]]** is very
resistant to corrosion — it stays "stainless" by self-coating,
exactly like the aluminium of the previous section. Uses follow
corrosion resistance: kitchen sinks, saucepans, knives and forks and
gardening tools, plus major industrial service in brewing, dairy and
chemical work, where corrosion-resistant vessels are essential.
Significantly more expensive than mild steel, it is bought only where
the corrosion bill justifies it.

| Type of steel | Iron mixed with | Some uses |
|---|---|---|
| mild steel | up to 0.25% carbon | nails, car bodies, ship building, girders |
| high-carbon steel | 0.6–1.2% carbon | cutting tools, masonry nails |
| stainless steel | chromium (and nickel) | cutlery, cooking utensils, kitchen sinks |

Copper completes the property-to-use catalogue, and every entry is an
examination favourite:

| Use | Property |
|---|---|
| electrical wires | very good conductor of electricity and ductile |
| pots and pans | very good conductor of heat, very unreactive and malleable |
| water pipes | unreactive — does not react with hot or cold water — and malleable |
| surfaces in hospitals | antimicrobial properties and malleable |

:::cross-curricular
This section is engineering economics in miniature. The car-body
decision between mild steel and aluminium weighs rust resistance,
density (fuel burn over the vehicle's life) and unit cost — a
three-factor trade-off argued exactly as a design engineer would.
The stainless-steel industry case (brewing, dairy, chemical plant)
shows corrosion chemistry setting capital budgets: vessels that
survive their contents are worth a premium alloy. Even the coinage
choice of cupronickel is monetary policy meeting metallurgy —
durability and cost per coin, struck billions of times.
:::

:::exam-hint
Steel-comparison questions are answered with *paired* properties:
mild steel for car bodies because strong, malleable and cheaper than
the alternatives; high-carbon for tools because harder and
wear-resistant, accepting brittleness; stainless where corrosion
resistance is worth the premium, with the chromium-oxide mechanism
stated. Two further marks hide in the details: density (mild steel
about three times denser than aluminium — the fuel argument) and
rusting (mild steel's disadvantage that stainless answers). Quote the
carbon percentages when asked to identify a steel — 0.25% versus
0.6–1.2% separates mild from high-carbon on sight.
:::

:::misconception
"Stainless steel never rusts because chromium is unreactive." The
chromium is *very* reactive with oxygen — that is the entire trick. It
reacts instantly to build the same kind of thin, strong oxide layer
that aluminium builds, and the layer seals the iron away from oxygen
and water. Unreactive metals resist corrosion by not reacting;
stainless steel resists corrosion by reacting first, once, at the
surface. Two different mechanisms with the same visible result —
confusing them loses the mechanism mark.
:::

:::summary
In one page: most metals are extracted from ores in the Earth's
crust; only unreactive metals occur uncombined (2.22C). Extraction
method follows the reactivity series — carbon reduction below carbon
(iron, with carbon monoxide as the furnace's working reducing agent),
electrolysis above zinc (aluminium in molten cryolite at around
1000 °C, cathode Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, anode 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻), reactive-metal
reduction for the awkward few such as titanium (2.23C) — and you
reason through any process from the two costs (energy, reducing
agent) plus the redox labels (2.24C). Uses follow properties:
aluminium (low density, conducts, self-protecting oxide layer) in
planes, cables and pans; copper (conducts, unreactive, malleable,
antimicrobial) in wires, pipes, pans and hospital surfaces; the three
steels — mild (0.25% C, strong and workable, rusts), high-carbon
(0.6–1.2% C, hard and brittle, tools), stainless (chromium, nickel;
self-protecting) (2.25C). An alloy is a metal mixed with one or more
other elements, usually metals or carbon (2.26C), and alloys are
harder because differently sized atoms break the regular lattice so
the layers of ions cannot slide (2.27C).
:::
